sections.title: Dock Appointment Planning
sections.en: 5.2 Dock Appointment Planning This section delves into a few scenarios with dock appointment planning: one scenario where the TU is created without yard management (which we’ll focus on in Section 5.2.1) and another scenario using yard management, where the TU is created in SAP EWM first (which we’ll cover in Section 5.2.2).

sections.title: Inbound Process in SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling
sections.en: 5.2.1 Inbound Process in SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling Let’s take a deeper look into the inbound goods receipt business process, specifically the scenario where a TU is created without yard management, based on dock appointment planning. In this business process, the dock appointment serves as a planning object and is first planned in the SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling module. The next step is the creation of a TU in SAP EWM. Business Process As shown in Figure 5.4, the business process for dock appointment planning without yard management involves the following steps: After receiving information about a delivery and its scheduled date, the carrier’s appointment planner logs on to SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling. Via the web-based application, this user creates an appointment for the delivery date. The appointment planner enters the warehouse’s docking location and the purchase order as a reference document. The system automatically calculates the loading point, appointment duration, and the number of required time slots based on the purchase order data. The carrier then selects a suitable start time slot. At least 1 day prior to the delivery date, the warehouse clerk reviews the scheduled appointments for the next day. This user ensures that enough capacity at the loading point is available to accommodate the planned 1 2 3 Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com 330 trucks for unloading. If necessary, the warehouse clerk reschedules the appointment or increases the available workforce in the warehouse. Upon the truck’s arrival, the driver provides the appointment number to the checkpoint clerk. The checkpoint clerk then searches for the appointment in SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling using the appointment number and changes the status to Arrived at Checkpoint. Subsequently, the checkpoint clerk finds an available door in SAP EWM, creates a planned door activity, and guides the truck to the designated door. The truck driver takes the delivery note to the goods receipt department, where a goods receipt office clerk locates the corresponding inbound delivery in SAP EWM. A warehouse worker confirms the truck’s arrival at the door and begins unloading the truck. A warehouse clerk cross-checks the goods with the delivery note and brings the revised delivery note to the goods receipt office. The goods receipt office clerk records the goods receipt, and the system automatically generates and prints warehouse orders for the inbound delivery. These warehouse orders facilitate the movement of goods into the warehouse. Subsequently, the truck leaves the door, and a warehouse clerk updates the status to Departed from Door. Figure 5.4 Dock Appointment Planning Creates TU without Yard Management The truck proceeds to the checkpoint, and the checkpoint clerk searches for the appointment in SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling using the 4 5 6 © 331 appointment number and then updates the status to Departed from Checkpoint. The warehouse worker transfers the goods from the goods receipt area to their respective storage types within the warehouse. Towards the end of the week or the month, the warehouse clerk selects all the appointments from the previous week or month in the Analyze Appointments screen to analyze the waiting and processing times as well as the disparities between planned and actual times. The warehouse clerk determines the number of trucks that arrived on time and whether the processing time aligns with the planned times. Configuration In this section, we’ll cover the key customization steps required for this process, assuming that the main SAP EWM customization settings have already been configured in the system: 1. Configure a docking location This configuration setting is required for the creation of a docking location in SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling. Users with an administrator role can follow the SAP NetWeaver menu path Dock Appointment Scheduling • Settings • Simple Setup • Simple Setup of Integrated Dock Appointment Scheduling • Create/Maintain Docking Location or use Transaction NWBC. To configure a docking location, input the warehouse number, click Continue, and maintain the Docking Location field, as shown in Figure 5.5. Figure 5.5 Configuring a Docking Location 2. Configure a loading point This configuration setting is needed to create loading points in SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling. Users with an administrator role can follow the 7 Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com 332 SAP NetWeaver menu path Dock Appointment Scheduling • Settings • Simple Setup • Simple Setup of Integrated Dock Appointment Scheduling • Create/Maintain Loading Point. Maintain the Loading Point and Docking Location fields as well as any other details required by your business processes, as shown in Figure 5.6. Figure 5.6 Configuring a Loading Point 3. Configure the determination of loading points This configuration setting is needed to configure how loading points are determined in SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling. Users with an administrator role can follow the SAP NetWeaver menu path Dock Appointment Scheduling • Settings • Simple Setup • Simple Setup of Integrated Dock Appointment Scheduling • Determine Loading Point or execute Transaction /SCWM/DSDETLP in SAP EWM. Click New Entries and maintain the Loading Point and Docking Location fields, as shown in Figure 5.7. Figure 5.7 Configuring Determination of Loading Point 4. Configure the determination of appointment duration This configuration setting is needed to configure how appointment duration is determined in SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling. Users with an administrator role can follow the SAP NetWeaver menu path Dock Appointment Scheduling • Settings • Simple Setup • Configure Appointment Duration Determination or execute Transaction /SCWM/DSCONFDUR in SAP EWM. Click New Entries and fill out the fields in © 333 the Configure Appointment Duration Determination section, as shown in Figure 5.8. Figure 5.8 Configuring Determination of Appointment Duration 5. Configure integration to other systems This configuration setting is needed for the integration settings of loading appointments when SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling is integrated to other systems, for example, SAP ERP or SAP S/4HANA. This configuration defines the SAP ERP system of the purchase order referenced in the loading appointment. Users with an administrator role can follow the SAP NetWeaver menu path Dock Appointment Scheduling • Settings • Simple Setup • Interfaces • Interface Settings for Dock Appointment Scheduling or execute Transaction /SCWM/DSINT in SAP EWM. Click New Entries and assign docking locations by maintaining the Docking Location and Business System for ERP fields and then select all three checkboxes, as shown in Figure 5.9. Figure 5.9 Configuring Integration to Other System 6. Configure assignment of door to a loading point This configuration setting is enables the assignment of doors to a loading point. Users with an administrator role can follow the SAP NetWeaver menu path Dock Appointment Scheduling Menu • Settings • Simple Setup • Simple Setup of Integrated Dock Appointment Scheduling • Assign Doors to Loading Points or execute Transaction NWBC. Then, maintain the Loading Point and Warehouse Number fields, as shown in Figure 5.10. Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com 334 Figure 5.10 Configuring Assignment of Door to a Loading Point 7. Configure time slots for the loading point This configuration setting defines the time slots of a loading point. Users with an administrator role can follow the SAP NetWeaver menu path Dock Appointment Scheduling • Settings • Simple Setup • Simple Setup of Integrated Dock Appointment Scheduling • Create Time Slots in Graphical View or execute Transaction NWBC, maintain the Loading Point, Start Date, and Time fields. Click Continue and create time slots as needed, as shown in Figure 5.11. Figure 5.11 Configuring Time Slots of a Loading Point 8. Configure an appointment planner for a carrier This configuration setting is needed to enable carrier appointment planners, who are external users, to book appointments directly in SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling. Using external web access, users with an administrator role can follow the SAP NetWeaver menu path Dock Appointment Scheduling • Settings • Simple Setup • Simple Setup of Integrated Dock Appointment Scheduling • Create Appointment Planners for Carrier or execute Transaction NWBC. Maintain the Carrier Number field and press (Enter). Then, configure individual appointment planners for the carrier by maintaining the Appointment… and User columns, and then click Save, as shown in Figure 5.12. © 335 Figure 5.12 Configuring an Appointment Planner for Carrier 9. Define control parameters for forming vehicles and Tus You can control how vehicles and TUs are formed in the system. In this configuration setting, the link between packaging material (of a TU) and means of transport will be defined. Follow the IMG menu path SCM Extended Warehouse Management • Extended Warehouse Management • Cross-Process setting • Shipping and Receiving • General Setting • Define Control Parameter for Forming Vehicles/Transportation Unit. Click New Entries and maintain the Means of Trans. field, as shown in Figure 5.13. Figure 5.13 Define Control Parameters for Forming Vehicles and TUs 10. Define a product group type In this configuration setting, a product group type will be defined. This product group type is assigned to product groups. Follow the IMG menu path SCM Extended Warehouse Management • SCM Basis • Master Data • Product • Product Group • Define Product Group Type. Click New Entries and maintain product group types via the ProdGrType and Description columns, as shown in Figure 5.14. Figure 5.14 Define Product Group Type Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com 336 11. Define a product group In this configuration setting, a product group will be defined. A product group type is assigned to a product group. Follow the IMG menu path SCM Extended Warehouse Management • SCM Basis • Master Data • Product • Product Group • Define Product Group. Click New Entries and maintain the Product Group field, as shown in Figure 5.15. Figure 5.15 Define Product Group Master Data Setup One primary master data setting needed for this process: maintaining the product group for the product master. Follow the SAP Easy Access menu path Logistics • SCM Extended Warehouse Management • Extended Warehouse Management • Master Data • Product Maintain Product or execute Transaction /SAPAPO/MAT1. Then, under the Properties 2 tab, maintain product group types and product groups for the product master, as shown in Figure 5.16. Figure 5.16 Product Master: Maintain Product Group for Product Master Process Demo In this section, we’ll go through an inbound goods receipt process using SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling step by step: 1. Create a purchase order in SAP ERP or SAP S/4HANA To create a purchase order, execute Transaction ME21N. Input the supplier, material, purchase order quantity, plant, and receiving storage location, and any other details required by your business process, and click Save, as shown in Figure 5.17. © 337 Figure 5.17 Create a Purchase Order in SAP ERP or SAP S/4HANA 2. Create an inbound delivery in SAP ERP or SAP S/4HANA To create an inbound delivery, execute Transaction VL31N and enter the Supplier and Purchase Order and other details, as needed, and click Continue and Save to generate an inbound delivery, as shown in Figure 5.18. Figure 5.18 Create Inbound Delivery with Reference to Purchase Order in SAP ERP or SAP S/4HANA 3. Create a loading appointment with reference to a purchase order in SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling To book the appointment in SAP NetWeaver, execute Transaction NWBC and select the Dock Appointment Scheduling tab. Then, click Maintain Appointment - Textual and enter a loading point sand reference document number and click Save to create the appointment, as shown in Figure 5.19. Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com 338 Figure 5.19 Create Appointment: Textual 4. Book a time slot for a loading appointment in SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling To book a time slot for an appointment in SAP NetWeaver, execute Transaction NWBC and select the Dock Appointment Scheduling tab. Then, click Create Appointment - Textual and select a planned arrival at checkpoint time to maintain the appointment and save, as shown in Figure 5.20. Figure 5.20 Maintain Appointment: Textual 5. Process a TU in SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling To process a truck at a checkpoint in SAP NetWeaver, execute Transaction NWBC and select the Dock Appointment Scheduling tab. Then, click Process Appointments and enter the loading point and appointment number from the previous step. sections.title: Dock Appointment Planning in SAP EWM
sections.en: 5.2.2 Dock Appointment Planning in SAP EWM In this business process, the TU is the processing object of the transport. A TU is assigned to outbound deliveries and linked to warehouse processing. This process involves the creation of the TU followed by appointment creation in SAP EWM. We’ll walk through both inbound and outbound processes in this section. Inbound Process Let’s focus first on the inbound goods receipt business process, specifically a scenario where the TU is created in SAP EWM with yard management along with dock appointment execution. Business Process As shown in Figure 5.27, the business process for inbound deliveries using SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling with yard management involves the following steps: 1. The process begins with the creation of an inbound delivery document (with reference to a purchase order) in SAP ERP or SAP S/4HANA. The inbound delivery is replicated to SAP EWM. A warehouse operator generates a TU in SAP EWM and associates the inbound delivery with it. These elements form the planned appointment in SAP EWM as well in SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling. Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com 342 Figure 5.27 Creation of TU (With Yard Management) 2. The appointment planner then determines the loading point and assigns a time slot for the provisional appointment. Afterwards, the provisional appointment is converted into a planned order within SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling. 3. Upon the TU’s arrival at the warehouse, the checkpoint clerk directs the truck to the assigned checkpoint. A warehouse operator further assigns the TU to a door. 4. The TU is unloaded and is directed to a checkpoint for release by a checkpoint clerk. 5. All yard movements, such as the ad-hoc moving of a truck or TU from a checkpoint to a door or parking area (and vice versa), take place in the system as yard management movements. Configuration In this section, we’ll utilize the configuration settings performed in Section 5.2.1. Now, we’ll walk you through dock appointment execution with yard management. Consequently, we’ll proceed by configuring some additional yard management-related settings: 1. Define a yard using a storage type In this configuration step, you’ll define a yard using a storage type by following the IMG menu path SCM Extended Warehouse Management • Extended Warehouse Management • Master Data • Shipping and Receiving • Yard Management • Define Yard Using Storage Type. Click © 343 Position and maintain the Warehouse No. field and other entries, as shown in Figure 5.28. Figure 5.28 Define Storage Types 2. Define the structure of a yard using storage sections In this configuration step, you can structure your yard using storage sections by following the IMG menu path SCM Extended Warehouse Management • Extended Warehouse Management • Master Data • Shipping and Receiving • Yard Management • Structure Yard Using Storage Areas. Click New Entries and maintain entries CHKN, CHKS, DOR1, and PSL1, as shown in Figure 5.29. Figure 5.29 Define Storage Sections 3. Define checkpoints To use yard management, you must define control points by following the IMG menu path SCM Extended Warehouse Management • Extended Warehouse Management • Master Data • Shipping and Receiving • Yard Management • Define Checkpoints. Click New Entries and maintain entries CHKN and CHKS, as shown in Figure 5.30. Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com 344 Figure 5.30 Define Checkpoints 4. Define warehouse doors In this configuration, you can define doors in a warehouse by following the IMG menu path SCM Extended Warehouse Management • Extended Warehouse Management • Master Data • Warehouse Door • Define Warehouse Door. Click New Entries and maintain entries, as shown in Figure 5.31. Figure 5.31 Define Warehouse Doors Master Data Setup In this section, we’ll go through primary master data settings needed for this process: 1. Create storage bins To create storage bins, follow the SAP Easy Access menu path Logistics • SCM Extended Warehouse Management• Extended Warehouse Management • Master Data • Shipping and Receiving • Yard Management • Create Storage Bin or execute Transaction/SCWM/LS01. Enter a warehouse number and a name for the storage bin in the Storage Bin field and save, as shown in Figure 5.32. © 345 Figure 5.32 Create Storage Bins 2. Assign a checkpoint to a yard bin and supply chain unit To assign a checkpoint to a yard bin and supply chain unit, follow the SAP Easy Access menu path Logistics • SCM Extended Warehouse Management • Extended Warehouse Management • Master Data • Shipping and Receiving • Yard Management • Assign Checkpoint to Yard Bin and SCU or execute Transaction /SCWM/YM_CHKPT_BIN. Assign the Storage Bin to the Checkpoint, as shown in Figure 5.33. Figure 5.33 Assign Checkpoint to Yard Bin and Supply Chain Unit 3. Assign a door storage bin and supply chain unit To assign a door storage bin and supply chain unit, follow the SAP Easy Access menu path Logistics • SCM Extended Warehouse Management • Extended Warehouse Management • Master Data • Shipping and Receiving • Assign Door Storage Bin and Supply Chain Unit or execute Transaction/SCWM/DOOR_SCU. Assign the Storage Bin to the Supply Chain Unit Door and Loading Point, as shown in Figure 5.34. Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com 346 Figure 5.34 Assign Door Storage Bin and Supply Chain Unit 4. Assign warehouse door to yard bin To assign a warehouse door to a yard bin, follow the SAP Easy Access menu path Logistics • SCM Extended Warehouse Management • Extended Warehouse Management • Master Data • Shipping and Receiving • Yard Management • Assign Warehouse Door to Yard Bin or execute Transaction /SCWM/YM_DOOR_BIN. Assign the Yard Bin to the Whse Door (warehouse door) and YrdWhseNo. (yard warehouse number), as shown in Figure 5.35. Figure 5.35 Assign Warehouse Door to Yard Bin Process Demo In this section, we’ll go through the inbound goods receipt and putaway process with SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling and yard management step by step: 1. Create a purchase order in SAP ERP or SAP S/4HANA To create a purchase order, execute Transaction ME21N. Input the supplier, material, purchase quantity, plant, and receiving storage location and other required details and save, as shown in Figure 5.36. © 347 Figure 5.36 Create Purchase Order 2. Create an inbound delivery in SAP ERP or SAP S/4HANA and create an HU To create an inbound delivery, execute Transaction VL31N, enter supplier and purchase order detail and other details as per your business requirements, and click Continue. Click Continue and confirm warehouse task, as shown in Figure 5.47. 13. Business Process The business process for outbound delivery using SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling with yard management involves the following steps: 1. As shown in Figure 5.50, to initiate the outbound process, a warehouse operator generates a TU within SAP EWM and associates it with the outbound delivery. This action automatically creates a provisional appointment in SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling. Figure 5.50 Dock Appointment Planning in SAP EWM: Outbound Process 2. The appointment planner then determines the loading point and assigns a time slot for the provisional appointment. Afterwards, the provisional appointment is converted into a planned order within SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling. 3. Upon arrival of the truck at the warehouse, the checkpoint clerk directs the truck to the assigned checkpoint in the system. Once the loading process is finished, the checkpoint clerk releases the truck from the checkpoint and authorizes its departure from the warehouse door. sections.title: Summary
sections.en: 5.3 Summary Great! You’re all set to start working on dock appointment scheduling. In this chapter, we provided an overview of SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling: You learned how it integrates with other systems and the necessary requirements for implementing SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling. We explored the process of receiving inbound goods using planning features in SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling. We walked you through the steps involved in scheduling dock appointments for incoming shipments and the benefits it brings to logistics processes. You learned about the planning aspect of dock appointments in an SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling system, both for inbound and outbound processes. We discussed how TUs are planned in SAP EWM. In addition, we explored various SAP roles and SAP Fiori apps that SAP has released specifically for the dock appointment scheduling functionality. These tools enable users to effectively manage and monitor dock appointments. By covering these topics, you should now have a comprehensive understanding of SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling, its integration with SAP systems, the inbound goods receipt process, planning in SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling, and other SAP tools available for managing dock appointments. © 361 6 Warehouse Automation Systems A warehouse automation system encompasses a meticulously coordinated amalgamation of components that, through synergy, optimize efficiency, precision, and productivity within the warehouse. Ranging from automated storage and retrieval systems and robotic picking systems to conveyors, sortation systems, warehouse management system (WMS) software, and automated guided vehicles (AGVs), these components spearhead progress in the industry, empowering businesses to meet the ever-mounting demands of the contemporary world. This chapter delves into an array of warehouse automation components that can be seamlessly integrated with SAP Extended Warehouse Management (SAP EWM). Moreover, we provide an extensive exploration of diverse automation system components, including material flow systems, warehouse robotics systems, automated storage and retrieval systems, and AGVs. The integration of SAP EWM with warehouse automation systems aims to create a seamless and tightly synchronized environment where manual and automated processes work in harmony. This integration enables businesses to leverage the benefits of automation technology while maintaining control and visibility over warehouse operations through a unified system. The integration of SAP EWM enables seamless data exchange, efficient process coordination, optimized resource utilization, and enhanced traceability. By leveraging the power of automation alongside a robust WMS like SAP EWM, organizations can achieve greater operational excellence and stay competitive in the fast-paced world of modern warehousing. This chapter commences by providing an overview of warehouse automation systems. We discuss detailed information about the different warehouse automation systems that are being utilized in state-of-the-art warehouses, as well as their integration with WMSs. Furthermore, we delve into the intricacies of the material flow system and its application in both inbound and outbound processes. sections.title: Overview of Warehouse Automation Systems
sections.en: 6.1 Overview of Warehouse Automation Systems In today’s fast-paced world of logistics, the demand for efficient and productive warehouse operations has never been greater. Thankfully, the advent of warehouse automation systems has brought about a transformative change in the industry. By integrating cutting-edge technology and advanced robotics, these systems have streamlined processes, minimized errors, and significantly increased operational efficiency. A warehouse automation system involves the implementation of different software and technologies to automate and streamline the various processes associated with managing and operating a warehouse. These technologies can include AGV systems, material flow systems, WMSs, conveyor systems, robotics systems, and automated storage and retrieval systems. Numerous businesses across various industries are using warehouse automation to optimize their supply chain management and improve overall productivity. The aim of warehouse automation is to enhance the efficiency, precision, and swiftness of warehouse tasks, while simultaneously minimizing costs and errors. By automating inventory management, order processing, and material handling activities, warehouse automation facilitates organizations to enhance their supply chain management and overall productivity. At the heart of a warehouse automation system are several key components working in harmony to optimize every aspect of the supply chain. First and foremost, automated storage and retrieval systems play a vital role. These systems utilize computer-controlled mechanisms to handle the storage and retrieval of goods, eliminating the need for manual intervention and maximizing space utilization. © 363 Next, robotic picking systems have emerged as game-changers. Equipped with sensors and advanced algorithms, these robots navigate through the warehouse, accurately identifying and picking items for order fulfillment. By eliminating human error and drastically reducing picking time, these systems have revolutionized the e-commerce sector. Conveyors and sortation systems are another integral part of warehouse automation. These systems transport goods seamlessly throughout the warehouse, ensuring timely and efficient movement from one area to another. They enable continuous flow and facilitate the sorting and routing of items based on predefined criteria, optimizing order processing. To manage and orchestrate these complex operations, WMSs provide the necessary intelligence. WMS software integrates with various components of the automation system, overseeing inventory control, order processing, and real- time tracking. This centralized control ensures smooth coordination and enhances visibility across the supply chain. Finally, to ensure a safe and secure working environment, AGVs have gained prominence. These autonomous vehicles navigate through the warehouse, transporting goods, and even interacting with other automation components. With built-in safety measures and efficient route planning, AGVs contribute to reducing accidents and improving operational efficiency. Businesses can utilize various types of automation systems to streamline their warehouse operations, which include the following: Conveyor systems These automated systems transport goods from one location to another within a warehouse. Automated storage and retrieval systems These systems utilize computer-controlled cranes to retrieve and store products in high-density storage systems. Robotics systems These systems employ robots for tasks like palletizing, depalletizing, and order picking. AGVs These unmanned vehicles transport products through the picking process, enhancing accuracy and speed. Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com 364 Automated packing systems These systems automatically package products for shipping. Automated labeling systems These systems label products with barcodes and other identifying information automatically. Sortation systems These systems sort and distribute products according to predetermined criteria. Pick-to-light systems These systems employ lights to guide workers through the picking process, which results in higher accuracy and speed. Pick by voice /augmented reality (AR) This warehouse automation system uses speech recognition technology to guide warehouse workers through the picking process. WMSs These systems manage and optimize warehouse operations, including inventory management, order processing, and shipping and receiving. In general, these automation systems can improve efficiency, increase productivity, reduce errors, and lower labor costs for businesses. Starting with SAP EWM 5.1, an integration option for automated warehouses has been available. This integration allowed for the connection of programmable logic controllers (PLCs) to various systems such as conveyor belts, rack feeders, lifts, and more through SAP EWM. One key aspect of integrating SAP EWM with warehouse automation systems is the exchange of real-time data and information. Automated systems such as conveyor belts, sorters, robots, and automated storage and retrieval systems are equipped with sensors and other technologies that capture data on inventory movements, order statuses, and equipment performance. This data is seamlessly shared with SAP EWM, providing accurate and up-to-date information for decision-making and process optimization. By integrating with warehouse automation systems, SAP EWM can effectively manage and orchestrate various automated processes. For example, it can control and monitor the movement of AGVs within a warehouse, ensuring efficient material flow and picking processes. It can also coordinate with robotic © 365 systems for tasks such as picking, packing, and palletizing, improving order fulfillment speed and accuracy. Furthermore, integration with warehouse automation systems allows SAP EWM to optimize resource utilization and warehouse layout. The system can analyze real-time data from automated equipment, such as storage capacity, equipment availability, and congestion points, to make intelligent decisions on task assignment, equipment allocation, and routing. This optimization minimizes unnecessary movements, reduces idle time, and maximizes the use of available resources, leading to improved throughput and operational efficiency. Another significant benefit of integrating SAP EWM with warehouse automation systems is enhanced traceability and visibility. Automated systems generate a wealth of data regarding inventory movements, picking and packing processes, and quality control. By integrating this data with SAP EWM, businesses can have a comprehensive view of their warehouse operations in real-time. They can track the progress of orders, identify bottlenecks, and proactively address any issues that may arise. Furthermore, SAP EWM can be integrated with various other warehouse automation systems, including the following: Material flow systems SAP Warehouse Robotics for robotic integration Automated storage and retrieval systems AGVs Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com 366

sections.title: Material Flow Systems
sections.en: 6.2 Material Flow Systems A material flow system, as shown in Figure 6.1, allows for the connection of an automatic warehouse to SAP EWM without requiring an additional warehouse control unit. The material flow system can be configured to divide warehouse tasks from a source location to a destination location into smaller subtasks. These subtasks are then transmitted step-by-step to a PLC, which is a real-time system responsible for controlling the physical transportation of handling units (HUs) and their components on the conveyor system. Figure 6.1 Overview of Material Flow Systems The communication between the material flow system and PLCs is facilitated through telegram communication. With this setup, the putaway and removal from storage of HUs can be accomplished without the need for additional software systems. Business warehouses can define the capacity limits for communication points, conveyor segments, or resources, and as a result, the SAP EWM system holds back tasks for the PLC as soon as these limits are being approached. A material flow system provides the following features: Identification of HUs is automatic through scanners in the automatic storage retrieval facility. HUs that cannot be stored due to incorrect contours, excessive weight, or lack of identification are automatically diverted. © 367 Fully automatic putaway of HUs in the storage bin is possible using any number of interim steps. These interim steps are represented by communication points. Malfunctions reported by the controls are taken into account. Capacity limits for communication points, conveyor segments, and vehicles are taken into account. Task interleaving is used to reduce empty traveling paths for stacker cranes. Goods-to-person picking is available. Stock is available for deliveries during transportation within the system. Parallel, bidirectional communication channels ensure stable telegram communications between SAP EWM and PLCs. In the following sections, we’ll discuss both inbound and outbound processes of the material flow system.

sections.title: Inbound Process
sections.en: 6.2.1 Inbound Process In this section, we’ll explore inbound processes using the material flow system in detail. The inbound process flow with a material flow system involves the movement of materials into a warehouse. The material flow system is a module within the SAP EWM solution for managing and optimizing material flows within a warehouse. Business Process As shown in Figure 6.2, an inbound process flow with the material flow system involves the following steps: 1. The inbound goods receipt process begins with creation of an inbound delivery with reference to a purchase order in SAP ERP or SAP S/4HANA. 2. As the truck physically arrives at the warehouse, the material is physically unloaded, and the warehouse operations team performs a goods receipt in the SAP EWM system. The goods receipt document records the actual receipt of the material in system and updates the inventory in SAP EWM as well as SAP ERP system. Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com 368 3. Posting a goods receipt in SAP EWM creates a warehouse task automatically, based on the postprocessing framework (PPF) configuration. The pallet HU is physically loaded at the scanner area, which is mapped to communication point. Pallet movement from the unloading area to the scanner area or communication point will vary depending on the business process. 4. Once the pallet HU is scanned for a weight and dimension check, communication between the PLC/conveyor system and SAP EWM start. The PLC communicates to SAP EWM about the current source location. SAP EWM confirms the message is received and communicates back to the PLC regarding the next destination location. 5. The pallet HU is moved from one communication point to another with reference to the creation and communication of the warehouse task between PLC and SAP EWM. 6. With the help of a crane, the pallet HU is finally putaway in an aisle bin, and the warehouse putaway process is complete. Throughout the inbound process flow, a material flow system provides real-time visibility and control over material movements, ensuring efficient and accurate handling of incoming goods within a warehouse. Figure 6.2 Inbound Process Material Flow System © 369 Configuration In this section, we’ll cover the primary configuration steps needed for inbound goods receipts using the material flow system: 1. Define the PLC interface type in SAP EWM To accommodate various devices such as pallet conveyors, case conveyors, single load handling devices, multiple load handling devices, shuttles, robots, or elevators, utilizing diverse telegram types and structures may be necessary. sections.en: 6.2.2 Outbound Process In this section, we’ll go through the outbound process using the material flow system in detail. Business Process The outbound process flow with a material flow system, shown in Figure 6.52, typically involves the movement of goods from the warehouse to a production area or a shipping area. The material flow system is a component of SAP EWM for managing and optimizing material flows within a warehouse. An outbound process flow with a material flow system generally involves the following steps: 1. The outbound goods issue process begins with the creation of an outbound delivery with reference to a sales order in SAP ERP or SAP S/4HANA. 2. This outbound delivery is automatically replicated to SAP EWM, and the SAP EWM system creates a wave with reference to the outbound delivery order. Upon release of the wave, the pick warehouse task is getting to move the material from the aisle bin to the outbound staging area. 3. With the SAP EWM-PLC interface, the SAP EWM system communicates to the crane PLC to pick the pallet HU from the source aisle bin and move to the next communication point. 4. The crane picks the pallet HU and physically moves to the next communication point and communicates back to SAP EWM about the HU move. © 393 Figure 6.52 Outbound Process with the Material Flow System 5. The SAP EWM system acknowledges the message and communicates the next destination location to the crane or conveyor PLC. 6. With the communication between SAP EWM and PLCs, and with reference to the creation and confirmation of warehouse tasks, the pallet HU finally moves to the outbound shipping area. 7. As the truck arrives, the loading of pallet the HU is performed, and the warehouse operation team performs the post goods issue for the outbound delivery order. sections.title: SAP Warehouse Robotics
sections.en: 6.3 SAP Warehouse Robotics SAP Warehouse Robotics simplifies the integration of robots, making their use as easy as plug-and-play. Although a new class of human-safe, collaborative robots is available from hundreds of low-cost vendors, challenges still exist related to software stack and system integration. SAP Warehouse Robotics helps users of SAP EWM to swiftly integrate nearly any warehouse robot, requiring only hours or days instead of weeks or months. The solution can be easily scaled as needed and enables the operation of diverse fleets using the same software stack. By integrating the latest generation of collaborative robots with SAP EWM, warehouse automation becomes affordable and effortless. SAP Warehouse Robotics has made agile robotics more accessible by offering the following features: Simple setup and scalability, with the ability to quickly add additional robots as needed to handle peak demand. Freedom from vendor lock-in, thanks to compatibility with a wide range of transportation robots commonly used in warehouses. This flexibility eliminates the need for expensive integration projects. Effortless management of diverse fleets, without the need for additional integration efforts. SAP Warehouse Robotics can be operated with out-of-the-box scenarios for SAP EWM. This resource provides simplified security and IT governance, lower costs, and easier entry into the world of warehouse robotics. Additionally, SAP Warehouse Robotics facilitates easy robot integration and allows for the addition of new ad-hoc robots. It also enables the management of heterogeneous fleets in one solution, where different robots can perform different tasks. SAP Warehouse Robotics allows warehouses to automate operations using robots. This approach enables HUs to be moved from source storage areas (storage bins) to destination storage areas (storage bins). SAP Warehouse Robotics can seamlessly integrate with warehouse robots from various vendors with minimal variations, enabling the operation of heterogeneous fleets. This solution provides strategic flexibility and a cost-effective entry point into the world of warehouse robotics. Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com 406 Other benefits include the following: With SAP Warehouse Robotics, users can expand into areas where robots were not previously utilized, particularly for non-repetitive and assistive tasks. This flexibility is particularly beneficial for small and medium-sized companies who previously could not afford robots. Furthermore, users can scale up and down ad-hoc to optimize machine usage. Finally, SAP Warehouse Robotics enables users to avoid vendor lock-in and operate fleets from multiple vendors without managing various software stacks. Various options are available to integrate robots with SAP Warehouse Robotics, including the following: Integration with services With this option, robots are integrated with SAP Warehouse Robotics through integration services specifically designed for SAP Warehouse Robotics, as shown in Figure 6.78. Figure 6.78 Integration with Services Integration with fleet management system This option involves integrating robots with SAP Warehouse Robotics through the fleet management system, as shown in Figure 6.79. © 407 Figure 6.79 Integration with Fleet Management System SAP Warehouse Robotics is a product that utilizes SAP Business Technology Platform (SAP BTP). By using SAP Warehouse Robotics, you can automate warehouse operations through the use of robots. For example, robots can be programmed to move HUs from one storage bin to another. Additionally, SAP Warehouse Robotics provides Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) that can be integrated with the fleet management systems of various robot vendors. To integrate SAP Warehouse Robotics with the fleet management systems of various robot vendors, an adapter must be implemented. This adapter serves as a bridge between SAP Warehouse Robotics and the fleet management system, enabling the following actions to be performed: Translation of robot tasks dispatched from SAP Warehouse Robotics into APIs within the fleet management system Writing back of robot task statuses from the fleet management system to SAP Warehouse Robotics An API for the fleet management system adapter consists of two methods: creating a robot task and updating a robot task status. Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com 408

sections.title: Automated Storage and Retrieval Systems
sections.en: 6.4 Automated Storage and Retrieval Systems An automated storage and retrieval system is a technology-driven solution designed to streamline inventory management in manufacturing warehouses and distribution centers. It integrates software technologies and hardware to automate the process of storing and retrieving goods from storage locations. Essentially, an automated storage and retrieval system can be thought of as a “mini-warehouse” within a larger warehouse, with bulk storage, small racks, and other storage areas arranged in a specific physical layout. The automated storage and retrieval system serves several purposes, including receiving and storing inventory from external sources, holding in-process inventory for production lines, managing inventory levels, and facilitating the retrieval of pallets for order picking and customer delivery. Typically, automated storage and retrieval systems utilize various storage technologies such as pallet racks, shelving, vertical lift modules, and carousels. These storage units are controlled by computer software that manages inventory and directs the movement of goods throughout the facility. The automated storage and retrieval process begins with the arrival of goods at the warehouse. The items are received and entered into the inventory management system, which determines the optimal storage location based on various factors such as size, weight, and demand. The automated storage and retrieval system then automatically retrieves the appropriate storage unit and transports it to a picking station where the items are removed and prepared for shipment. The advantages of an automated storage and retrieval system include increased efficiency, improved accuracy, and reduced labor costs. It also helps to minimize the amount of space required for storage, enabling companies to optimize the use of floor space in the warehouse. We’ll discuss the two automated storage and retrieval system integration options in the following sections. © 409

sections.title: Integration with a Material Flow System
sections.en: 6.4.1 Integration with a Material Flow System Automated storage and retrieval systems and material flow systems are two important systems used in the manufacturing and warehousing industry. The automated storage and retrieval system is used for automated storage and retrieval of goods, while the material flow system is used for managing the material flow in a warehouse. To interface between these two systems, the following technical details must be considered: Communication protocol The automated storage and retrieval system and the material flow system communicate through a standard communication protocol. Commonly used protocols include OPC-UA (Open Platform Communications - Unified Architecture) and TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol). The protocol used for communication will depend on the specific requirements of the warehouse. Data exchange The automated storage and retrieval system and the material flow system exchange data in real time. The automated storage and retrieval system provides information on the locations and statuses of goods, while the material flow system provides information on the demand for goods and their destinations. The exchange of data is done through the communication protocol, and the data is processed by the respective systems to update their own databases. Interface development The interface between the automated storage and retrieval system and the material flow system needs to be developed based on the specific requirements of the warehouse. The interface can be developed using middleware tools, such as production integration, or using custom-developed software. The interface should be designed to handle the exchange of data in real time and should be scalable to handle large volumes of data. An automated storage and retrieval system and a material flow system can be integrated with each other by developing an interface between them. This interface typically involves developing custom code or middleware to facilitate the exchange of data between the two systems. The interface may use APIs, web services, or other integration technologies to connect the two systems. Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com 410 System integration Once the interface is developed, the automated storage and retrieval system and the material flow system must be integrated. This step involves connecting the systems to the interface, configuring the communication protocol, and testing the interface to ensure that it is functioning correctly. Error handling The automated storage and retrieval system and the material flow system must be designed to handle errors that may occur during the data exchange. For example, if the automated storage and retrieval system fails to provide the location of a product, the material flow system should be able to handle this error and take appropriate action. In summary, the interface between the automated storage and retrieval system and the material flow system involves the development of a communication protocol, data exchange, interface development, system integration, and error handling. These technical details should be carefully considered to ensure that the interface is functioning correctly and can handle the requirements of your warehouses.

sections.title: Integration with Automated Guided Vehicles
sections.en: 6.4.2 Integration with Automated Guided Vehicles The integration of an automated storage and retrieval system with AGVs can greatly enhance the efficiency and productivity of a warehouse or distribution center. By combining the storage and retrieval capabilities of an automated storage and retrieval system with the autonomous transportation capabilities of AGVs, you can create a highly automated and streamlined material handling system. At a high level, the integration works in the following way: Automated storage and retrieval system An automated storage and retrieval system consists of a series of racks, shelves, or bins that can store and retrieve items automatically. It typically uses robotic cranes or shuttles to handle storage and retrieval tasks. The automated storage and retrieval system is connected to a central control system that manages inventory, tracks locations, and handles orders. AGVs AGVs are autonomous vehicles designed to transport goods within a warehouse or distribution center. They can navigate throughout a facility © 411 using various technologies such as lasers, magnetic strips, or vision systems. AGVs are equipped with sensors for obstacle detection and can communicate with the central control system. Integration The integration between the automated storage and retrieval system and AGVs involves coordination between the two systems. The central control system of the automated storage and retrieval system communicates with the AGVs to instruct them on the locations of items to be retrieved or stored. Retrieval process When an order is received, the central control system identifies the location of the requested item within the automated storage and retrieval system. It then sends instructions to the AGVs, specifying the location and item details. The AGVs navigate to the designated rack or shelf and wait for the automated storage and retrieval system to retrieve the item. Item retrieval The automated storage and retrieval system system’s robotic cranes or shuttles retrieve the requested item from the designated storage location. Once the item is retrieved, the automated storage and retrieval system communicates with the AGVs to inform them that the item is ready for transport. Transport The AGVs receive the signal from the automated storage and retrieval system and navigate to the location where the item was retrieved. They load the item onto their platforms or trailers and transport items to the desired destination, such as a packing area or a specific workstation. Storage process When items need to be stored in an automated storage and retrieval system, the central control system identifies an available storage location. It sends instructions to the AGVs, specifying the item details and the destination rack or shelf. The AGV transports the item to the designated location and waits for the automated storage and retrieval system to store it. Item storage The automated storage and retrieval system’s robotic cranes or shuttles receive items from AGVs and place these items in a designated storage location within the automated storage and retrieval system. The automated Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com 412 storage and retrieval system then updates its inventory records accordingly and communicates the completion of the storage task to the AGVs. System optimization The integration of automated storage and retrieval system with AGVs allows for real-time optimization of material flows within a facility. The central control system continuously monitors the inventory, order status, and AGV locations to optimize the allocation of storage and retrieval tasks, minimize travel distances, and maximize operational efficiency. By integrating automated storage and retrieval system with AGVs, you can achieve a seamless and efficient material handling system, reducing manual labor, improving accuracy, and increasing overall productivity in warehousing and distribution operations. © 413

sections.title: Automated Guided Vehicles
sections.en: 6.5 Automated Guided Vehicles AGVs are autonomous vehicles used to transport materials or products within manufacturing warehouses or distribution environments. They are equipped with sensors, navigation systems, and control systems so they can move around a facility without human intervention. AGVs can follow predefined paths or use real-time mapping and localization to navigate around obstacles and other vehicles. The journey of AGVs has been a long one, starting from simple trucks and culminating in modern laser-guided AGVs. An AGV is a mobile robot that follows predefined paths or series of paths, typically along the floor of a manufacturing or warehouse facility, to transport materials or goods. These vehicles are designed to operate autonomously and are guided by various technologies such as magnetic tape, lasers, or cameras. AGVs are used in various industries such as manufacturing, automotive, aerospace, pharmaceuticals, and logistics to move materials and products efficiently and safely. They can be programmed to move goods between different locations, such as between storage areas, assembly lines, or shipping docks, without requiring human intervention. AGVs come in different forms, including forklifts, pallet trucks, and carts, and can be powered by batteries, electric motors, or a combination of both. Some AGVs are equipped with sensors so they can detect obstacles in their paths and avoid collisions, making them safe to operate around humans and other machinery. AGVs come in many shapes and sizes, from small, simple machines to large, complex vehicles capable of carrying heavy loads. They can be designed to transport goods on flat surfaces, to move up and down ramps, or to enter and exit elevators. AGVs follow predefined paths and handle battery charging separately. On average, in most industries, AGVs require 12 minutes of high-speed charging per hour of usage. AGVs can adapt to options such as wireless charging, automatic battery swaps, or solar-powered batteries to quickly get back to business. AGVs use various forms of sensors and signals to guide them to their destination. These sensors can range from a computer vision system that builds a real-time Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com 414 view of the plant, with obstacle detection and collision avoidance algorithms, to a wire or coded tape on the floor defining a more static route. While many types of AGVs and navigation methods exist on the market, they all use some form of sensor and signal system to tell the AGV where it is located in the space, where it needs to go, and how to get there. Overall, AGVs are a cost-effective solution for automating material handling tasks in various industries, improving efficiency, reducing labor costs, and enhancing worker safety. AGVs are becoming increasingly popular in warehouses and distribution centers due to their ability to automate material handling tasks, increase efficiency, and reduce costs. By integrating AGVs with SAP EWM software, material flows and warehouse operations can be further optimized and synchronized. To integrate AGVs with SAP EWM, follow these steps: 1. Develop a communication interface between SAP EWM and the fleet management system (control system/guidance system) of the AGV system manufacturer or vehicle. This step enables the distribution of warehouse tasks to AGVs and supports the communication of warehouse task confirmations back to SAP EWM. SAP EWM supports various communication protocols for integrating AGVs, such as TCP/IP, XML, or APIs as well as IDoc communication. 2. Configure the AGV as a resource in SAP EWM. AGVs are treated as resources in SAP EWM, which can be reserved, scheduled, and tracked like any other warehouse resource. The AGV is defined as a resource with its own set of characteristics, such as maximum speed, capacity, and location. 3. Create and schedule AGV tasks. AGV tasks (transport requests) can be created in SAP EWM using standard transactions or through a custom interface. These tasks can include picking up and delivering materials, replenishing inventory, and moving empty containers. The tasks are then scheduled based on the availability of the AGV and the priority of the task. AGVs physically pick up the HU from the conveyor system and deliver it to the staging area. The SAP EWM system sends a warehouse task to the AGV, and the AGV confirms the warehouse task back to SAP EWM as the HU stages to the intended location specified by SAP EWM. 4. Monitor and control AGV operations. SAP EWM provides real-time visibility into the status of AGV tasks, allowing warehouse managers to monitor and © 415 control AGV operations. This visibility includes tracking the AGV’s location, speed, and battery level, as well as receiving alerts if any issues or delays arise. 5. Integrate with other warehouse processes. AGVs can be integrated with other warehouse processes, such as inventory management, order management, and quality control. For example, AGVs can be used to automatically move materials from a receiving dock to storage locations or to transport materials from one workstation to another. Additionally, SAP EWM can communicate with the AGV controller software using its APIs, making it the central brain for orchestrating activity and providing a digital command center for the entire operation, as shown in Figure 6.80. Most companies typically initiate their integration with an AGV system by linking it with their SAP EWM system. This connection provides insight into the inventory available, its location within a facility, and the quantity of each item present in a specific location. As SAP EWM usually comes equipped with an interface, a standard operating procedure for a minimal integration can be developed to simply record the removal of materials from a particular location in the warehouse and its placement onto an AGV. The AGV will then add it to the new location where it is delivered. Figure 6.80 AGVs Imagine the AGV as a forklift driver given a list of items to pick. You can either arrange the storage area such that the AGV can collect known quantities of items on pallets, or you can have a staff member responsible for selecting and loading materials onto the AGV. Once the AGV is loaded to its capacity, it moves to the Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com 416 next location, unloads itself or is unloaded, and proceeds to the subsequent destination. If you want to integrate AGVs with your warehouse system, you must connect to the AGV system’s API. This API is necessary to send the AGVs information about where they need to go, what they should pick up, and when they should complete each task. Depending on the AGV supplier, you’ll either need a standalone interface to manage these tasks or API endpoints that you can use with other software packages to exchange information with your AGVs. The documentation for the AGV system will outline how this system operates. Although the specifics may differ, the general idea is that you’ll transmit information to the API (such as work order numbers, pick and place locations, AGV type required for the operation, preferred routes, and schedule). The API will then interact with the AGVs, informing them of what to do and when to do it. © 417

sections.title: Summary
sections.en: 6.6 Summary Thus concludes our discussion of warehouse automation systems. Throughout this chapter, we delved into various aspects, beginning with the overview of warehouse automation systems. Furthermore, we explored inbound and outbound processes using material flow systems. Additionally, we examined the most interesting and important topic of warehouse automation and explored options for integrating warehouse automation systems with SAP EWM. Finally, we touched upon several warehouse automation topics, such as automated storage and retrieval systems and AGVs and their integration option with SAP EWM. Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com 418 7 Yard Logistics SAP Yard Logistics, an all-encompassing software solution provided by SAP, offers a holistic approach to optimizing and managing logistical operations in yard or terminal settings. Its primary objective revolves around enriching the efficiency, visibility, and coordination of inbound and outbound logistics activities encompassing transportation, storage, and goods handling. This chapter provides an overview of the integration between SAP Extended Warehouse Management (SAP EWM) and SAP Yard Logistics. Yard logistics refers to the management of operations that take place within the confines of a shipping yard, such as a warehouse, distribution center, or freight terminal. These operations typically involve the movement of goods, vehicles, and personnel within the yard, as well as the storage and retrieval of items. Yard logistics can also involve coordinating and tracking the movement of shipments, scheduling delivery times, and managing the flow of vehicles and people in and out of the yard. Effective yard logistics is critical for ensuring the efficient and timely movement of goods and materials within the supply chain. Warehousing and transportation meet at yards, which act as the connecting link. The integration of SAP EWM and SAP Yard Logistics seamlessly facilitates the synchronized orchestration and optimization of warehouse operations alongside yard management. Consequently, enterprises can adeptly administer inbound and outbound logistics processes, while adeptly handling the movement and storage of goods within warehouse and yard premises. In essence, the harmonious convergence of SAP EWM and SAP Yard Logistics enables a streamlined flow of goods, engenders heightened operational efficiency, and augments the visibility and command over warehouse and yard undertakings. Ultimately, this amalgamation empowers organizations to attain amplified logistics efficiency, culminating in the provision of superlative customer service. We’ll begin this chapter with an overview of the yard logistics process and walk through the SAP Yard Logistics solution and its integration with SAP EWM. Then, we’ll cover using SAP Yard Logistics in depth, detailing both inbound and outbound processes. ©

sections.title: Overview of Yard Logistics
sections.en: 7.1 Overview of Yard Logistics The yard logistics process involves a number of steps, including the following: Receiving goods The process typically starts with the receipt of goods into the yard. This step can involve checking the goods against the shipping manifest, ensuring that the correct quantities and items have been received, and organizing the goods for storage or further distribution. Storage and retrieval Once the goods have been received, they must be stored within the yard. This step involves finding an appropriate location within the yard to store the goods and ensuring that they are stored safely and securely. When the goods are needed for distribution or transportation, they must be retrieved from storage. Inventory management Effective yard logistics also requires careful inventory management. This step involves keeping track of the quantities and locations of items within the yard, as well as monitoring the flow of goods in and out of the yard to ensure that inventory levels are maintained. Equipment and personnel management Yard logistics also involves managing the equipment and personnel needed to move goods within the yard. This step can include coordinating the use of forklifts, pallet jacks, and other handling equipment, as well as managing personnel schedules and ensuring that workers are trained and equipped to carry out their duties safely and efficiently. Transportation management Finally, yard logistics also involves coordinating the movement of goods into and out of the yard. This step can include scheduling deliveries and pickups, coordinating with transportation providers, and ensuring that goods are transported in a timely and efficient manner. Businesses across various sectors and industries, engaged in the movement of goods through logistics and supply, have come to acknowledge that transportation disruptions frequently occur not just on the road, but also when resources are situated in the yards of your manufacturing plants and distribution centers. Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com 420 Effective yard logistics requires careful planning, coordination, and execution of these processes in order to ensure that goods are moved through the supply chain in a safe, efficient, and cost-effective manner. The efficiency of modern manufacturing operations and warehouses can be hampered by various inefficiencies in their yards, such as the following: Inadequate visibility into shipments and trailers, making it difficult to shuttle them between plants and distribution centers. The availability of space is a major challenge for yard management, particularly in urban areas where land is scarce and expensive. Limited space can make it difficult to accommodate large numbers of vehicles and shipments and can also impact the speed and efficiency of operations. Shipping delays for inbound and outbound goods. Poor management of yard trailers, leading to higher expenses on spotters and shuttles. Challenges in locating empty trailers to meet outbound load schedules. Delayed truck driver pickups. Traffic congestion is another common challenge in yard management, particularly in busy transportation hubs such as ports and airports. Congestion, particularly at entry and exit gates, can slow down operations, increase waiting times for drivers, and result in delays and increased costs. Effective communication is crucial in yard management, particularly when coordinating activities with carriers, drivers, and other stakeholders. Poor communication can lead to misunderstandings, delays, and safety issues. Insufficient visibility into the arrival of shipments at destination facilities. Yard management also involves ensuring the safety and security of personnel, equipment, and shipments. This goal can be challenging, particularly in high- traffic areas where there is a risk of accident, theft, and damage. You may have limited ability to monitor safety and compliance violations. Many yard management operations are still reliant on manual processes and paper-based systems, which can be time consuming and prone to errors. Integrating technology such as radio frequency identification (RFID) and GPS can help streamline operations and improve visibility, but integrating these technologies can also be a complex and costly process. © 421 Extreme weather conditions, such as snow, rain, and wind, can impact yard operations and cause delays and safety issues. Preparing for and managing these conditions requires careful planning and coordination. To remain competitive in global markets, companies with yards must implement professional logistics processes that are supported by a highly integrated and user-friendly system across the entire supply chain. The use of SAP Yard Logistics can provide comprehensive support for transportation units (TUs) from check-in to check-out, with a focus on planning, execution, yard operations, monitoring, and billing functionalities. SAP Yard Logistics serves as the crucial link that connects transportation management, extended warehouse management (EWM), and SAP ERP. To successfully complete yard processes, several key features of SAP Yard Logistics are essential, including the following: Seamless integration with SAP Transportation Management (SAP TM) and SAP EWM Proper classification of TUs SAP Dock Appointment Scheduling Efficient task planning Cross-docking capabilities Accurate location determination Mobile yard execution for flexibility and mobility Integration with SAP Environment, Health, and Safety Management (SAP EHS Management) Proper classification of TUs Effective exception handling Comprehensive checking and measuring of activities Mobile yard execution for flexibility and mobility Streamlined internal yard processes Real-time monitoring and alerting Easy printing of relevant documents Convenient driver self-service check-in Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com 422 Effective exception handling Internet of Things (IoT) enablement and integration capabilities Easy printing of relevant document Accurate billing of yard tasks SAP Yard Logistics is a powerful tool that effectively manages, controls, and streamlines transport processes and vehicle movements within the plant premises, commonly known as the yard. Through its advanced 2D and 3D graphical layouts, SAP Yard Logistics enables real-time monitoring and visualization of the current situation on site, providing complete transparency at all times with regards to all goods-moving and transport-relevant processes in the yard By integrating SAP Yard Logistics into other SAP solutions such as SAP EWM, SAP TM, and SAP Business Network for Logistics, manual processes can be eliminated, leading to the optimization of logistics processes. This integration results in enhanced efficiency, reduced errors, and improved customer satisfaction. As shown in Figure 7.1, SAP Yard Logistics offers several benefits, including the following: SAP Yard Logistics provides maximum transparency when it comes to yard processes, resulting in improved efficiency and productivity. It significantly reduces check-in and check-out times and optimizes the use of assets and yard areas. Through tracking functions, it reduces truck waiting times, and by monitoring and alerting, it identifies bottlenecks in the process. SAP Yard Logistics also offers cross-docking functions for combined delivery and collection, which increases efficiency and reduces costs. The solution can track and trace vehicles as well as swap bodies, trailers, and containers within a yard, which leads to greater control and management of resources. With its advanced yard automation features, such as scoreboards, RFID, and GPS, it enables IoT scenarios and provides greater visibility into yard operations. Planning yard activities is a fundamental basis for yard automation, and SAP Yard Logistics streamlines this process by automating tasks and integrating with other SAP solutions such as SAP EWM and SAP TM. In this way, it optimizes yard operations, reduces errors, and improves customer satisfaction. © 423 Figure 7.1 SAP Yard Logistics Overview SAP Yard Logistics is available in two versions to suit different organizational needs: Add-on for SAP S/4HANA Enterprise Management The first variant is as an add-on for SAP S/4HANA Enterprise Management, which provides organizations with a comprehensive solution for managing their yard logistics operations. The add-on is fully integrated with SAP S/4HANA and provides users with real-time visibility into all yard activities to optimize yard operations. Standalone SAP S/4HANA application The second variant is a standalone SAP S/4HANA application that can be connected to either an SAP S/4HANA Enterprise Management or a legacy enterprise resource planning (ERP) system. This option allows organizations to use SAP Yard Logistics as a standalone solution, enabling them to manage their yard logistics operations separately from their other ERP processes. Both variants of SAP Yard Logistics as shown in Figure 7.2 provide organizations with a range of features and capabilities, including real-time visibility into yard operations, advanced planning and scheduling, automated processes, and enhanced collaboration among all stakeholders. Organizations can choose the variant that best suits their specific requirements and business processes. Figure 7.2 SAP Yard Logistics Deployments Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com 424 The functional comparison highlights the benefits of SAP Yard Logistics over yard management in SAP EWM. How can you ascertain whether investing in the SAP Yard Logistics solution is necessary or if yard management in SAP EWM is sufficient for managing your business? Table 7.1 lists the drivers between SAP Yard Logistics and yard management. SAP Yard Logistics Yard Management in SAP EWM Multimodal transportation modes (which can only be achieved with proper infrastructure, which may require significant investments if not already available) Efficient yard operations (which may require minimal automation and potentially limited willingness to invest) Heightened complexity Streamlined yard processes Automated yards Table 7.1 Functional Comparison between SAP Yard Logistics and Yard Management SAP Yard Logistics and SAP EWM are two separate SAP solutions that can be integrated to create an end-to-end warehouse management system (WMS). The following the integration options between SAP Yard Logistics and SAP EWM are available: SAP Yard Logistics can be integrated with SAP EWM to create inbound and outbound deliveries for managing goods receipt and goods issue processes. This integration allows for the seamless transfer of data between the two systems and ensures that all warehouse movements are tracked and managed efficiently. In addition to supporting planning and operational processes, SAP Yard Logistics facilitates integration scenarios (using sample integration functionality) in conjunction with either SAP ERP, SAP TM, or SAP EWM. In conclusion, integrating SAP Yard Logistics and SAP EWM can provide organizations with a comprehensive and efficient WMS that can streamline their operations and improve their supply chain performance. © 425 Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com 426

sections.title: Using SAP Yard Logistics
sections.en: 7.2 Using SAP Yard Logistics In this section, we’ll provide a detailed explanation of SAP Yard Logistics. We’ll begin with the inbound process and cover the outbound process as well. For both scenarios, we’ll walk through the business process, configuration, and master data setup needed then provide a process demonstration.

sections.title: Inbound Process
sections.en: 7.2.1 Inbound Process The purpose of the inbound logistics process with SAP Yard Logistics is to streamline the flow of goods and materials into a company’s operations, ensuring efficient operations, reducing costs, and enhancing customer satisfaction. We’ll look at the inbound process in detail in the following sections. Business Process As shown in Figure 7.3, the inbound process using SAP Yard Logistics involves the following steps: 1. The first step in the inbound goods process is to create a purchase order for a vendor in SAP ERP or SAP S/4HANA. The purchase order is then converted to an inbound delivery, which is automatically distributed to SAP EWM for warehouse processing. 2. Once the planning is complete, the shipment is distributed to SAP EWM as well as SAP Yard Logistics to trigger the process of truck arrival, loading, and departure. The message from SAP ERP or SAP S/4HANA triggers the creation of the yard request in SAP Yard Logistics, which is used to plan the first yard activity. 3. At the same time, the message from SAP ERP or SAP S/4HANA is also sent to SAP EWM, a dependent document is created, namely the TU, which contains information about the planned content. In addition, an automatic door determination or manual door assignment occurs, allowing SAP EWM to begin the putaway and staging process. Note that, since SAP EWM and SAP Yard Logistics are involved in this process, no yard activities, such as check- in postings or movements, will be executed. These steps fall within the scope of SAP Yard Logistics. © 427 Figure 7.3 Inbound Process Using SAP Yard Logistics 4. While the warehouse begins its activities in SAP Yard Logistics, the yard order is created based on the yard request, which is used for processing in the yard. In an inbound scenario such as this, an inbound yard order will be created. For the departure of the truck, an outbound yard order is required, which can be generated from the inbound yard order. 5. Meanwhile, in SAP EWM, the inbound process is performed, and the products are unloaded and putaway. At the same time, different yard activities are taking place in SAP Yard Logistics. Once the movement to the door is activated, another door determination may occur. This step is used when no door determination was triggered earlier or to validate the previously determined door. 6. With confirmation of the yard task in SAP Yard Logistics, the arrival at the door will be posted in SAP EWM. At this point, the TU can no longer be moved in the yard. Activities in the yard will only be possible again after receiving notification from SAP EWM that the unloading has been completed. 7. This notification triggers yard operations to start the movement from the door to the next yard location, such as the checkpoint for departure. A message about this pending departure from the door is sent from SAP Yard Logistics to SAP EWM. Meanwhile, the goods receipt can be triggered in SAP EWM. The latest point for a goods receipt posting is during the check-out of the TU. Again, after the unloading notification has been sent to SAP Yard Logistics, no further yard activities are allowed in SAP EWM. All postings happen in SAP Yard Logistics. Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com 428 8. Now that the truck has reached the inbound checkpoint, the check-in can be posted. This check-in will also be sent to SAP EWM, triggering the check- in posting there. Based on the goods receipt and check-in posting in SAP EWM, SAP ERP or SAP S/4HANA documents will be updated. Configuration In this section, we’ll cover the key configuration required for this process, assuming that the basic configuration in SAP EWM, SAP ERP, or SAP S/4HANA, and SAP Yard Logistics have already been performed in the system: 1. Assign SAP EWM business systems and warehouses to yard in SAP Yard Logistics This configuration setting is required to integrate SAP Yard Logistics with SAP EWM. Follow the IMG menu path Yard Logistics • Integration • Integration to SAP Extended Warehouse Management • Assign SAP EWM Business Systems and Warehouses to Yard. Click New Entries and maintain the entry or entries or verify that these settings meet your business requirements, as shown in Figure 7.4. Figure 7.4 Assign SAP EWM Business Systems and Warehouses to Yards 2. Maintain SAP EWM checkpoints in SAP Yard Logistics This configuration setting is to maintain checkpoints. Follow the IMG menu path Yard Logistics • Integration • Integration to SAP Extended Warehouse Management • Maintain EWM Checkpoints. Click New Entries and maintain the entry or verify that these settings meet your business requirements, as shown in Figure 7.5. © 429 Figure 7.5 Maintain SAP EWM Checkpoints Master Data Setup Let’s delve into the master data setup required for an inbound goods receipt process using SAP Yard Logistics, which involves the following: 1.
